question: A patient on intramuscular diclofenac (not oral) for post-operative pain develops a gastric erosion. Which mechanism explains why NSAID gastropathy occurs even with parenteral administration?

answers.text: Systemic COX-1 inhibition reduces prostaglandin-mediated gastric mucosal cytoprotection regardless of the route of administration

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. NSAIDs inhibit COX-1 systemically wherever they reach via the bloodstream. COX-1 in the gastric mucosa produces PGE2 and PGI2 that maintain mucosal defence (mucus, bicarbonate, blood flow). Removing this cytoprotection — whether the NSAID is given orally, parenterally, or rectally — leads to mucosal erosion. The injury is prostaglandin-mediated, not contact-mediated.

answers.text: The injected drug is secreted into the stomach via biliary excretion, causing direct mucosal contact

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While some NSAIDs undergo enterohepatic recirculation, direct mucosal contact is NOT the primary mechanism of NSAID gastropathy. The injury occurs even with formulations that bypass the GI tract entirely (e.g. IV ketorolac), confirming it is a systemic effect of COX-1 inhibition on prostaglandin-dependent mucosal protection.

answers.text: Parenteral NSAIDs stimulate gastric COX-2, increasing pro-inflammatory prostaglandins in the stomach wall

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: NSAIDs inhibit, not stimulate, COX enzymes. NSAID gastropathy results from inhibition of constitutive COX-1 in the gastric mucosa, which removes prostaglandin-dependent mucosal defence — not from COX-2 stimulation.

answers.text: Intramuscular injection causes a stress response that independently increases gastric acid secretion

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While stress can increase gastric acid, this is not the mechanism of NSAID gastropathy. The injury is a direct pharmacological consequence of systemic COX-1 inhibition removing prostaglandin-mediated mucosal protection, occurring predictably with any route of NSAID administration.

overallFeedback.feedback: NSAID gastropathy is a systemic effect of COX-1 inhibition, not local irritation. COX-1-derived prostaglandins (PGE2, PGI2) maintain gastric mucosal defence — mucus, bicarbonate, and mucosal blood flow. Inhibiting COX-1 anywhere in the body removes this protection, regardless of the route of drug administration.

Excellent. This systemic mechanism explains why enteric-coated or injectable NSAID formulations do not prevent gastropathy — only COX-2 selective agents or PPI co-prescription can meaningfully reduce the risk.
